(e) The abstract places the phrase right after "accuracy falls in every run", which includes GSM8K Run C (−12.1 matched) and train-on-gold (−25.6/−25.9), both outside 5–11. So the scope of "5–11" is unclear. (f) Table 7's "Finished" decomposition part, a different quantity, is only −2.7 to −6.0 at the same rate. Readers may mix the two up, and the abstract does not say which one it reports. Suggested wording: "in a post hoc matched comparison, finished generations of verifier-filtered runs at the highest rate are 5.5–9.1 points less accurate (one of four intervals reaching zero)".

Related: Abstract's '5–11 points' covers only some of the runs that 'every run' refers to — The abstract says 'At the highest rate accuracy falls in every run, and finished solutions become 5–11 points less accurate'. The 5–11 range (5.5–10.6 in Table 5) comes from the six MATH-500 verifier-filtered and no-filter runs. Other runs at 5×10−4 fall outside it. Train-on-gold loses 25.6 and 25.9 points of matched finished accuracy, and the GSM8K Run C at 5×10−4 loses 12.1. Read literally, 'every run' at the highest rate includes those three, so the range is too narrow. Saying 'the six MATH-500 self-training and no-filter runs' would fix it. The intro states its scope correctly ('what training at the highest rate changes ... 5.5–10.6'), but the abstract does not.

comments.title: Rate dependence and 'cap-hit rises only at 5×10⁻⁴' are weaker than stated, and partly contradicted by the replicate and Table 12
comments.quote: at seed 1 sample accuracy falls 1.5, 3.5 and 8.3 points
comments.explanation:
The values are correct (Table 5: −1.5, −3.5, −8.3 at seed 1; −3.7, −3.8, −4.7 at seed 2), and the appendix hedges ('suggestive, not established'). But the main text's 'may grow with the rate on one seed' leans on the −8.3 endpoint, and the same-configuration replicate at seed 1 and 5×10⁻⁴ gives −5.2 (Table 7). The −8.3 run is therefore an extreme of two draws differing by 3.1 points, the paper's only replicate-noise estimate. That spread exceeds the 2-point gap between 1e-4 and 2e-4 at seed 1. Table 12 is also hard to square with a rate trend. Re-scored on the same seed-1 exam, the 2×10⁻⁴ adapter's deficit to the untrained model (−7.8 at 512 tokens) is as large as the two 5×10⁻⁴ adapters' (−8.0, −8.8), and its proxy-degenerate share (28.7%) is similar to theirs (30.0%, 37.2%). Likewise, §4.4's 'The cap-hit share rises only at 5×10⁻⁴' is true only at seed 2: at seed 1 the 5×10⁻⁴ rises (+3.0 [−1.7, 7.7], +2.3, replicate −0.2, 1024-limit +0.7) are within noise, as Appendix H itself notes. The main text should say the rate dependence is not supported beyond noise at either seed, and that the cap-hit rise is a seed-2 phenomenon.

Related: Introduction and Contribution 4 present the cap-hit rise without the conclusion's "clearly only at one seed" caveat — The introduction says what appears at the highest rate is lower finished accuracy "and more generations that run out of tokens". Contribution 4 says "the cap-hit share rises only at that rate". Both read as a finding that holds across runs at 5×10−4. App H and Table 7 show otherwise: at seed 1 the rise in A (+3.0 [−1.7, 7.7]) and no-filter (+2.3 [−2.5, 6.8]) has an interval including zero, "about the size of two samplings of the untrained model", and the replicate (−0.2) and the 1,024-limit run (+0.7) "do not rise at all". Termination contributes "clearly only at one seed", and the cap-share part ranges from 12–30% to 52–72% depending on seed/partition. The conclusion and App H state this correctly. The introduction and Contribution 4 should carry the same caveat (e.g. "rises clearly only at the highest rate and at one of two seeds"). Otherwise the front matter suggests a robust termination effect that the evidence does not support.

comments.title: The main text presents redundant measures as extra evidence: added/lost counts restate pass@k, and the 'four pre-set measures' include non-gain measures
comments.quote: 500 run but one, the problems lost equal or outnumber those gained.
comments.explanation:
§5.1 lists 'the problems lost equal or outnumber those gained' as a separate supporting fact. §3.4 and I.1 both note that added minus lost equals 150×∆pass@k, so this 'restates the sign of the pass@k change rather than adding evidence'. That caveat appears in the appendix but not in the main-text answer, where the sentence reads as corroboration. Likewise, the Conclusion says 'on the four measures fixed in advance no run improves detectably'. Of the four pre-set measures (pass@1, pass@k, style counts, added/lost; §3.4), style is not a gain measure and added/lost duplicates pass@k, so the null actually rests on two measures: pass@1, a single draw, and pass@k. Presenting four suggests a broader and more independent null than the data give. This is a case where a main-text summary of an appendix drops a qualifier that changes how strong the evidence looks. Suggested fix: add the 'restates pass@k' caveat to §5.1 (or drop the sentence), and in §7 name the gain measures (pass@1 and pass@k) rather than 'the four measures'.

Related: Added/lost counts appear as supporting evidence in §5.1, although §3.4 says they are not an independent test — §3.4 notes that added minus lost equals 150×Δpass@k, 'so these counts add only the gross churn behind the net change, not an independent test'. I.1 likewise says the count 'restates the sign of the pass@k change rather than adding evidence'. The main-text answer in §5.1 drops this qualifier and places the sentence right after the 2.2-point bound, as a further reason for 'Not detectably'. A reader of the main text alone would take it as extra evidence. It is the sign of Δpass@k, which Table 5 already reports with intervals, mostly including zero. The I.1 qualifier should be added to §5.1, or the sentence removed.

Related: "On the four measures fixed in advance no run improves detectably": two of the four measures have no notion of improvement or no interval — The four pre-set measures (§1) are pass@1, pass@k, \boxed style share, and per-problem transitions. Only pass@1 and pass@k have bootstrap intervals (Table 5), so "detectably" is defined only for them. Style is not a measure of mathematical improvement at all. Transitions are reported as raw added/lost counts with no interval, and §5.1 states that "In every MATH-500 run but one, the problems lost equal or outnumber those gained". For example, Run A seed 3 at 10−4 has 16 added / 14 lost (Table 4), a net gain on that measure. The conclusion's sentence extends a claim established for two measures to all four. It should say "neither pass@1 nor pass@k improves detectably in any run, and transitions are net-negative in all but one MATH-500 run".

comments.title: Abstract calls both controls "underpowered"; the no-filter control is dose-confounded, not underpowered, and shows a directional result
comments.quote: that patch a rarer defect or remove the filter are underpowered and show
comments.explanation: "Underpowered" fits the \dfrac patch, whose treatment changes 0–4 training examples (§4.3, App F). It does not describe the no-filter control. That control changes the training data massively (1,400 unfiltered examples against about 440 filtered, 3–4× the optimizer steps), so its problem is a dose/data confound, not a weak treatment (App G: "dose and data differ at once"). It is also not simply "no consistent difference": removing the filter lowers pass@4 at both seeds (−2.0, −5.3), and one sample-accuracy interval excludes zero in favour of the filter (−5.5 [−9.2, −1.8] at seed 2). The conclusion describes this more accurately ("removing the filter lowers pass@4 at both seeds, within noise; single-seed intervals sometimes exclude zero"). The abstract should say the no-filter control is confounded by dose and weakly favours the filter on pass@4.

comments.title: The verifier conclusions skip what the no-filter arm and the r_t null say about Egashira et al.; 'no consistent difference' undersells a filter that never helps
comments.quote: The defensible statement about the verifier is narrow: removing a format
comments.explanation: §5.2/I.2 settle on 'removing a format defect present in under 1% of generations, or removing the filter entirely, made no consistent difference', and say that whether systematic false negatives are harmless 'as Egashira et al. find for RLVR, our data cannot say'. Two points make this reasoning incomplete. (1) Removing the filter is not a false-negative manipulation. It turns roughly 70% of training examples into false positives (wrong answers), the error type Egashira et al. find can cause plateau or collapse. The no-filter arm is never better than the filtered arm and is worse at seed 2 (sample accuracy −10.2 vs −4.7; pass@4 lower at both seeds). With 3–4× the dose this cannot be attributed causally, but 'no consistent difference' is a flat summary of a one-sided pattern. The fact that training mostly on wrong solutions does about as well as training on verified ones is itself informative: either the filter adds nothing at this dose, or the recipe dominates (see the positive-reference issue). Neither reading is discussed. (2) The r_t result is the paper's one measurement bearing on a systematic false negative, and it is qualitatively in line with Egashira et al.'s finding that systematic FNs act like noise and are not exploited. The Discussion says the data 'cannot say' anything about this while the Abstract claims 'the model does not adapt to this defect'. The paper should either explain why the r_t null does not bear on Egashira's FN finding (e.g., different paradigm, untested avoidability), or note the consistency with suitable hedges. It should also discuss the no-filter result as a false-positive manipulation.

comments.title: 'Restart-from-base leaves compounding little room' contradicts the data-mediated compounding the paper itself argues for in Design P, and I.2 says the shrinking-pool mechanism has 'no support'
comments.quote: round leaves compounding little room, so the absence of compounding is
comments.explanation: J.7 and §6 present restart-from-base as limiting compounding. That holds only for parameter-level compounding. In the loop as described (§3.1), the round-t pool is generated by the round-(t−1) model, which was itself trained on a pool from the round-(t−2) model, so selection effects can still compound through the data. Appendix D says exactly this: dose 'explains at most the level of the decline, not its time course' (the largest drops come from the smallest pools), and 'Something carried through the data, such as pool composition or style, fits this acceleration better.' That is the self-reinforcing shrinking-pool mechanism, or close to it. Yet I.2 says 'The data give it no support, but they do not rule it out either', and §5.2 says they 'neither support nor rule it out'. The appendix offers some support (accelerating decline with shrinking pools, falling \boxed share, rising $-spans), even if it is not causal evidence, while the Discussion denies any support. Separately, if compounding through data is possible, the 'absence of compounding' in Design I cannot be put down to the restart design. It reflects the short loop (2–4 trained rounds), the small changes at 10^−5, and the lack of a frequent varied defect. Suggested fix: make §5.2/I.2 and App D say the same thing ('weakly consistent with but not tested'), and rewrite J.7 to separate parameter compounding (removed by the design) from data compounding (still possible, and suggested by Design P).

comments.title: Missing or understated limitations: the learning-rate comparison is confounded with k, pool size and number of rounds, and there is only one model family (Qwen2.5), the family where spurious-reward gains are known to appear
comments.quote: The learning-rate grid is coarse, with three
comments.explanation: §6 and J.4 call the higher-rate grid 'coarse' with three rounds and k = 4, but leave out the consequence. Rate is not the only thing that changes across the grid. At 10^−5 the runs use k = 8 and five rounds (round-0 pool 872, about 436 steps). At the higher rates they use k = 4 and three rounds, R0–R2, which is only two trained adapters (pool about 440, about 220 steps), and 'last round' is R4 in one case and R2 in the other (Table 5). So the higher-rate arms have about half the dose and half the training rounds of the 10^−5 arms. The pass@k measure also differs (pass@8 vs pass@4), so ∆pass@k is not comparable across rates. This matters for I.1 and App D, which use 'stronger training produces larger declines' across rates as indirect support for a dose explanation of the Design P collapse: across the grid, rate and dose move in opposite directions. J.7's 'at most five rounds' also hides that most conditions have two trained rounds, which limits any compounding test (see related issue). On scope, §6 says 'one model size in Design I' but not 'one model family'. The paper motivates itself with Shao et al.'s finding that random rewards raise accuracy (§1, §5.3), a result widely reported to depend strongly on Qwen2.5 models. Contamination of MATH-500/GSM8K (J.11) is also a known concern for Qwen2.5 specifically. Whether a sub-2B model 'learns mathematics or the verifier' under GVT may well depend on the family, so this belongs in the scope limitation, next to a note that the across-rate dose-response argument is confounded.

comments.title: Some practical suggestions are unsupported or contradicted by the paper's own evidence, and the most important lessons are left out
comments.quote: 0.5% of the pool cannot be detected with 150 problems
comments.explanation: I.3 rightly says that some suggestions are general good practice, but several are still written as findings. (1) 'A treatment that changes 0.5% of the pool cannot be detected with 150 problems' is a quantitative power claim with no power analysis behind it. The patch null shows non-detection, not undetectability: a small pool change could in principle have a large effect if those examples are influential. (2) 'Check that the training step changes the model (loss and output statistics after one round)' sits awkwardly with J.4, which reports that at 10^−5 'its loss does fall' while outputs barely change. On the paper's own evidence, loss is not a valid check, and only output statistics are. (3) The list leaves out the lessons the paper's evidence supports most directly: run a positive control (or at least a gold-SFT reference that improves) before reading a null (J.12, K); set the training sequence limit to at least the generation cap plus the prompt, since 24–26% of the kept pool is truncated (J.9), which plausibly teaches unfinished outputs; and give an equivalence margin in advance (J.10). (4) 'Hold out evaluation items and keep one adapter per dataset' is offered as a remedy for the Design P artefact, but App D argues selection-set scoring did not hide a decline and may have enlarged one, so the suggestion's basis is ordinary good practice, not the paper's data. Suggested fix: label each suggestion as finding-backed or general practice, and replace the loss check with output statistics.

comments.title: Table 11 gives the same round-0 length for two different exam partitions
comments.explanation: In Table 11, both 10−5 rows (A, seed 0 and A, seed 1) have round-0 mean length 1158 characters (1158 →1147 and 1158 →1146). Seeds 0 and 1 draw different 150-problem exam partitions, and their round-0 cap-hit shares (46.9% vs 40.7%) and finished accuracies (54.8% vs 55.2%) differ. With cap-hit six points apart, an identical mean length to the character is unlikely. Elsewhere, different partitions give different round-0 lengths (1175, 1154, 1178). This may be a transcription error and should be checked.

comments.title: "They do not ask what the gain consists of" is contradicted by the cited RLVR papers themselves
comments.quote: These studies improve accuracy, which our SFT loop does not, but they do not ask what the gain consists of.
comments.explanation: The first cited example is Wang et al.'s 36.0%→73.6% on MATH-500 (verified, https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.20571, NeurIPS 2025). Its own abstract decomposes that gain: it reports an '8.6% improvement beyond format correction', which implies most of the jump is format correction. That is the same 'mathematics or format/verifier?' question this paper poses, answered in part by the cited authors. In the sibling cluster, SimpleRL-Zoo (arXiv:2503.18892) analyses response length, reasoning behaviours and format-reward effects across its ten base models. Huang et al. (arXiv:2505.22203), from the same group, studies how rule-based-verifier false negatives shape RL gains. The statement is therefore inaccurate as written. It also hides a useful fact for the paper's motivation: the headline 1.5B RLVR number cited in §1 and §2 is largely a format effect by its authors' own account. That supports the paper's framing better than the current wording, which presents 36.0→73.6 as an unexamined accuracy gain. Suggested change: report the 8.6-point beyond-format figure, and narrow the claim to 'do not test whether the gain reflects adaptation to the verifier's specific defects'.

comments.title: Qiao et al. described as purely theoretical and out of its multi-silo setting
comments.quote: Qiao et al. [8] argue theoretically that a selector seeing only a narrow slice of the target distribution accelerates collapse.
comments.explanation: Qiao et al. (arXiv:2606.13732, ICML 2026, https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.13732) prove the result and also run experiments. Their setting is siloed selection, where each of several verifiers or institutions sees only a local, biased slice and raw data cannot be pooled, and they propose Wasserstein proxy references as a fix. 'Argue theoretically' undersells the empirical part. Leaving out the multi-silo framing makes the result look more directly applicable to a single rule-based verifier with a format bias than it is. A single format-biased verifier is a different kind of selection bias: it depends on the answer form, not on a local view of the distribution. This is minor, but the main-text paraphrase 'a narrow selector can accelerate collapse' should state the setting.

comments.title: 'The adapter barely changes the outputs' at 1e-5 rests on coarse aggregates and conflicts with the paper's own decline and divergence evidence
comments.quote: on MATH-500 the adapter barely changes the outputs (length and cap-hit share
comments.explanation: This claim carries a lot of weight. It is used to say the flat MATH-500 curve at 1e-5 is uninformative (§4.2), to explain the null patch control (§4.3, App F: 'nearly identical pools would give nearly identical models'), and it motivates the higher-rate runs (§4.4). The only evidence given is that mean length (1158->1147) and cap-hit share (46.9->47.4%, 40.7->41.8%) barely move for Run A. Those are coarse summaries: an adapter can change which answers are produced, the reasoning, or the style while leaving length and termination unchanged. The paper's own data show outputs did change in ways that matter. Finished accuracy goes 54.8->51.0 (Table 11). Matched finished accuracy falls 3.8 and 4.2 points with intervals excluding zero at seed 0. All-agree shares fall (14.6->12.0%). The paper reads the decline as a 'possible small decline', which implies the model changed. Either the 1e-5 declines are real, and then the adapter changed the outputs, or the outputs did not change, and then the declines are noise. The paper uses both readings in different places. The supporting evidence that 'the adapter therefore learns' (training loss 0.72->0.38) is also weak for this purpose: §3.4 says loss is computed over the whole chat sequence including the fixed prompt, so part of that drop may just be fitting the repeated template. To support the claim, a direct output-level measure is needed, for example \boxed/$ style shares by round at 1e-5 (as reported for the higher rates), per-problem added/lost churn compared with a resampling-of-base baseline, or token-level divergence between round-0 and round-4 generations. Otherwise 'little change' should be stated as an inference from length and cap-hit only.

comments.title: 'Little change is a property of rate and steps together' is concluded from a comparison confounded by dataset
comments.quote: is therefore a property of rate and steps together, not of the rate alone. A flat
comments.explanation: Appendix E concludes that 'little change' depends on steps as well as rate, because Run C, at the same rate with about twice the steps (951 vs 436), does change its outputs. Run C is also the only GSM8K run. It differs from Run A in dataset, in base accuracy (66.7% vs 32%), and in cap-hit regime (3.5% vs 41–48%). The same appendix and §4.2 explicitly decline to attribute Run C's decline to the dataset alone, for exactly this reason. Attributing Run C's larger output change to steps is the mirror-image inference and needs the same hedge. Run C's time course also does not fit a per-round dose effect well: 9.3 of its 12.7 pass@1 points are lost in the final round, while the per-round dose is roughly constant or shrinking. App D then cites this inference ('Run C ... is the one 10^-5 run that declines clearly') as support for the Design P dose reading, so the conclusion rests on a single confounded comparison. It should be stated as one possible reading, not as a finding.

comments.title: The 'dose explains level, not acceleration' argument is a false dichotomy, and dose does not even explain the level at round 1
comments.quote: Dose also explains at most the level of the decline, not its time course: with a
comments.explanation: The arithmetic checks out: the two largest pass@1 drops (-12.1 = 44.5->32.4 and -13.8 = 32.4->18.6) come from models trained on the pools of 3,395 and 2,638 examples. The inference drawn from it does not hold. (a) Dose and compounding through data interact rather than compete. Under restart-from-base, a larger per-round dose makes each round's model imitate its pool more strongly, so whatever drift is in the pool passes into the next generation faster. A high dose can therefore produce acceleration even while pool sizes shrink, so 'dose explains at most the level' does not follow. (b) The level is not explained by dose either. The round-1 model received the largest dose (3,962 examples, about 4.5x Run A) yet fell only 3.8 points (50.0->46.2), about the same as Design I Run A's round-1 drop of 2.7–5.3 points at 1x dose. On the dose reading the early level should differ most, and it does not. Together these suggest the collapse emerges over rounds, which fits a data-borne compounding mechanism amplified by dose more than either alone. The paper reaches a similar view ('something carried through the data ... fits this acceleration better'), but its stated reason splits the two mechanisms. The 1.5B pool shrinks by 60% (3,962->1,566) while the 0.5B pool shrinks only 16% (2,533->2,123); this is a further signal of compounding that could be used and is not discussed.

comments.title: The 0.5B Design P run is the natural within-design control but is underused and has no uncertainty attached
comments.quote: declines only a little, though it is a different model. Pooling or scoring may also
comments.explanation: The 0.5B and 1.5B Design P runs share both structural features the paper lists as alternative explanations: pooled training on one adapter, and scoring on the selection set. The 0.5B run also has a large dose (2,533 examples, about 2.9x Run A, not far from the 1.5B's 4.5x). It shows only a mild, roughly linear decline (pass@1 -3.7, pass@8 -5.6) and little pool contraction. This is the strongest evidence in the paper that pooling and selection scoring are not sufficient on their own to produce the collapse. Yet App D closes with 'Pooling or scoring may also have contributed' without confronting it, and dismisses the 0.5B comparison only with 'it is a different model'. Several things are missing for 0.5B that are given for 1.5B: a per-dataset split (Table 9), style counts, a per-round pool trajectory (only the endpoints 2,533 to 2,123), and any interval on its decline. The main text calls the decline 'small' with no interval, even though the paper insists elsewhere on bootstrap intervals and patterns across runs. Either analyse the 0.5B run as the partial control it is, which narrows the candidate causes to model-by-dose interaction or compounding, or state clearly that it was not analysed and why.

comments.title: Answer-diversity measures: stated scope contradicted by reported values, and the handling of cap-hit (no-answer) generations is unspecified
comments.quote: (0.542 →0.554 for Run A, seed 0; 0.528 →0.543 for Run B, seed 1) but rises
comments.explanation: App F says diversity was measured 'for Design P's 1.5B run and the 10^-5 Design I runs at seed 0'. The distinct-answer fraction is then reported for 'Run B, seed 1', which lies outside that scope. Either the scope or the label is wrong, and A and B are compared at different seeds and different partitions. More substantively, 41–48% of MATH-500 generations hit the token cap and mostly have no extractable answer, and in Design P \boxed usage halves. Neither the all-agree measure nor the distinct-answer measure says how a missing or unextractable answer is counted: as its own 'answer', as distinct each time, or excluded. That choice can by itself drive the reported movements, for example Design P's distinct fraction rising 0.443->0.712 and all-agree falling 24.8->1.7% as formatting drifts. The paper notes the link to cap-hits but gives no rule. Mixing selection and exam problems in Design I also mixes problems the model trained on with held-out ones. The paper draws no conclusion from these measures, which is appropriate, but the definitions need to be given for the numbers to be interpretable or reproducible.

comments.title: Table 2's round-3 pass@8 corresponds to the default preset, contradicting 'the two presets gave identical pooled values'
comments.quote: identical pooled values; a later per-dataset recomputation differs by one prob-
comments.explanation: App D says Table 2 was computed during the run, 'where the two verifier presets gave identical pooled values'. Table 9's caption says that after recomputation the pooled round-3 pass@8 is 63.5% under the reward preset (the one used for selection, and per §3.4 the definition of 'correct') and 63.6% under the default preset. 63.6% is the value in Table 2. Recomputing from Table 9's per-dataset reward values gives (82.2+44.8)/2 = 63.5. So Table 2's R3 pass@8 matches the default preset rather than the reward preset. This is a one-problem difference with no effect on conclusions, but the 'identical' statement and the convention that 'correct' means the reward preset are not exactly true for Table 2. The caption could say which preset Table 2 uses. All other Table 2 entries reproduce exactly as averages of Table 9's two datasets, and all Table 2, 3 and 9 deltas recompute correctly.

comments.title: 'Mostly real' argument for the train-on-gold decline is not bounded by the checks offered
comments.quote: fall of about 19 points, and finished accuracy falls to 12–15%, so we think the fall
comments.explanation: The concern is that the gold-trained model shifts strongly in format ($-spans 5%→98%, \boxed 52%→86%), and the same verifier grades the result. The paper offers three supports. (i) An exact-string match on boxed answers recovers 14/600 and 11/600 (≈2.3 and 1.8 points; checked). This is a lower bound, and the paper says so. (ii) The gold-storage re-score fixes a different defect, which the paper also concedes. (iii) Finished accuracy falls to 12–15% (Table 11: 14.7, 12.5). But (iii) is not independent evidence: finished accuracy is graded by the same verifier, so if the new style is misparsed it is misparsed in finished generations too. Nothing bounds the error from above. The ≈14% of round-2 generations with no \boxed are where math-verify falls back to the last LaTeX/$ span, and in a $-heavy reference style that span is often not the final answer. Those generations alone could account for up to ~14 points, and with the 2-point lower bound that is ~16 of the ~19-point fall. Equivalent-but-not-string-equal boxed answers are also uncounted. 'Even several times the first bound' is an arbitrary multiplier, not a bound. The conclusion may well be right, but a hand audit of a small random sample (e.g. 50 rejected round-2 generations per seed) is needed to support 'mostly real'. Otherwise the claim should be weakened to 'the share of verifier error is unmeasured; at least ~2 points of it is recoverable'.

comments.title: No-filter control confounds more than dose (62% truncated training data), and learning-rate dependence is used as evidence that step count matters
comments.quote: matter (the rate dependence above is suggestive), dose and data differ at once
comments.explanation: The no-filter vs Run A deltas check out from Table 6 (pass@1 +4.0/−4.7, pass@4 −2.0/−5.3; sample-acc +0.2/−5.5 from Table 5's round-0 values). Two problems remain. (a) The paper names only optimizer steps (700 vs 220/196, 3.2–3.6×) as the confound. Table 11 shows a second, mechanistically relevant one: 62.4% of the no-filter round-0 pool is longer than the 512-token training limit, against 24.5% for Run A. The no-filter model is thus trained mostly on examples with no final answer and no EOS, the very mechanism §H tests with the 1,024-limit arm. A 2.5× higher share of unterminated training data, plus unfiltered wrong answers, plus 3–4× the steps, makes the comparison uninterpretable as an effect of the filter. That it nonetheless barely differs from Run A at seed 1 (cap-hit +2.3 vs +3.0) is itself informative about the truncation hypothesis and deserves mention. (b) The justification 'since dose may matter (the rate dependence above is suggestive)' conflates learning rate with number of optimizer steps. The rate sweep varies step size at a fixed step count, so even a firm rate dependence would not show that step count matters. Recommend listing truncation share as a confound and dropping or rephrasing the rate→dose inference.

comments.title: Attribution between 'less accurate' and 'not finishing' rests on post-treatment conditioning and an untested counterfactual
comments.quote: round-0 samples (6–21 problems, 34–37 in the gold runs), which, being mostly
comments.explanation: The decomposition is arithmetically sound. I checked that the three parts sum to Δacc in every Table 7 row within rounding, and reproduced A seed 1 from Table 11 (s̄=0.553, Δf=−11.0 → −6.1; implied c=7.0%→4.7% → cap-acc −1.0; Δs=−3.0 × (f̄−c̄)=42.7 → −1.3). The interpretation is less secure, for three related reasons. (1) The matched metric conditions on finishing, an outcome of training. It drops the 22–45 problems (15–30% of the exam) where every last-round sample hits the cap, i.e. the problems most affected by non-termination. Within a problem, it also compares the round-0 finished samples with a different, selected subset at the last round, since when more samples run long, the ones that still finish are not a random draw. Matching on problem does not remove that within-problem selection. (2) The fallback baseline (all-sample round-0 accuracy for 6–21 problems, 34–37 for gold) is mostly cap-hit accuracy (4–7%). This biases the baseline down and so understates the matched decline. The paper notes the bias but not its direction for the headline '5–11 points'. In the gold runs a quarter of the problems use the fallback, so −25.6/−25.9 mixes two baselines. (3) The cap-share part Δs(f̄−c̄) values every generation that stops finishing at the average finished accuracy f̄. That assumes newly unfinished generations would have been as accurate as typical finished ones, but drift-prone generations are plausibly harder or already going wrong, which would make the termination share an overstatement. Conversely, the unmatched f in the finished part contains composition shifts. The 'Fin. share' percentages therefore depend on these assumptions as much as on the data. The text is careful ('descriptive'), but the abstract's 'mostly via less accurate finished solutions, partly via more cap-hits' framing should be stated as dependent on this counterfactual, and the direction of the fallback bias should be stated.

comments.title: The 1,536-token re-score points to non-termination at seed 1, contrary to 'picture unchanged'
comments.quote: cap leave the picture unchanged, within the noise of single runs (Appendix H).
comments.explanation: At 512 tokens, the seed-1 anatomy says finished accuracy carries most of the decline (finished part 73–89% for A, replicate and 1024-limit; cap-share 12–30%). Table 12 at 1,536 tokens tells a different story for the same seed-1 adapters. Proxy 'Acc. finished' is nearly identical across rows (untrained 44.1, replicate 43.3, 1024-limit 41.3, 2e-4 40.8), while the 'Degenerate' share is 2.5% vs 23–33%. The arithmetic shows that the deficit is almost entirely the degenerate share. With degenerate generations scored ≈0, sample acc ≈ (1−deg)×acc_fin: untrained 0.975×44.1=43.0 (reported 43.2); replicate 0.77×43.3=33.3 (34.2); 1024-limit 0.673×41.3=27.8 (29.5). The −9.0 replicate deficit is thus ≈0.205×43 ≈ 8.8 points of non-termination and <1 point of finished accuracy. The proxy undercounts cap-hits, which contaminates 'Acc. finished' with low-accuracy unfinished text more for the adapters, so their true finished accuracy is if anything closer to the untrained model's. The appendix does say the re-score 'points to non-termination', but §4.5 summarises it as leaving the picture unchanged. With a larger budget the seed-1 adapters look like models that fail to stop, not models whose finished solutions are 5–9 points worse. That conflicts with the 512-token seed-1 split and with the abstract's emphasis on less accurate finished solutions. A second caveat: the untrained 512-token re-score (36.3%) is 2.6 points above the run's own round 0 (33.7%), inflating all deficits. For example, the 2×10⁻⁴ deficit is −7.8 here against −3.5 in Table 5. The §4.5 sentence should be revised, and the anatomy claim qualified by cap length.

comments.title: 'Three rounds' and per-round step counts include a round-2 pool that trains no evaluated model
comments.quote: 175, against 220, 196 and 163 for Run A at seed 1 (and 212, 193, 175 at seed 2).
comments.explanation: Rounds are R0 (untrained), R1 (adapter on the R0 pool) and R2 (adapter on the R1 pool), so 'three rounds' at the higher rates means only two trained adapters, and each restarts from base. Yet the dose comparison lists three per-round step counts (220, 196, 163 = 440/2, 391/2, 326/2), and Tables 6/10 report a round-2 kept pool (326/350). The round-2 pool can only train an R3 adapter, which is never evaluated. Either a third adapter was trained and not reported, or the 163/175 figures are not optimizer steps behind any reported model. The steps relevant to the comparison are 220 and 196 (seed 1), giving 3.2–3.6× for no-filter and 0.8–0.9× for gold. These are consistent with '3–4×' and 'about the same', so the conclusion survives, but the listing invites the misreading that R2 reflects three rounds of training. Because of restart-from-base, the R2 model is one 196-step adapter trained on R1 outputs, not cumulative training. That should be stated wherever 'three rounds' or 'dose' is discussed (e.g. 'three evaluation points, two self-training iterations').

comments.title: FN audit: the 'wrong-token extraction' diagnosis is probably confounded with the gold-storage defect, and the 7.8% has a restricted denominator and no interval
comments.quote: the false-negative rate is 7.8% (10 of 128) on MATH-500
comments.explanation: §3.2 says 'most failures are wrong-token extraction from a long solution'. The basis for the label is that 8 of 10 cases are 'accepted when only the boxed answer is' verified. Appendix B says most of these 8 are compound answers (3\sqrt{13}, 6−5i, 11\sqrt{2}, ...) and overlap with the bare-gold class. This raises a confound the paper does not rule out. If the extracted answer is passed without its box delimiter, it may be parsed exactly as the bare gold is (to its first number), and then match by accident. On that reading, the 'boxed-only accepted' test would show the gold-storage defect, not a long-solution extraction failure. The paper hedges that 'the two labels describe where the failure shows', but the main text still states the extraction diagnosis, and it presents the gold-storage defect as a separate post hoc discovery the audit apparently already saw. Also: the denominator keeps only answers the authors' normaliser recognises as correct (128 of 176). Compound answers are where both the normaliser and math-verify are weakest, so FN on exactly the problematic class is probably understated. The audit uses Qwen2.5-7B solutions, not the loop's outputs. And a Wilson interval is given for GSM8K 0/200 but not for MATH-500 10/128, which is roughly [4.3%, 13.8%]. The authors should state exactly what string was passed in the 'boxed-only' check, give the interval, and reconcile 7.8% with the loop's 15.5–18.4%, most of the gap probably being the unparseable-gold overlap.

comments.title: Unparseable golds 'cancel within a partition' only for level offsets in differences, not for relative effects, conditional metrics or cross-partition comparisons
comments.quote: which lowers absolute pass rates but cancels
comments.explanation: The 51 unparseable golds (11–18 per exam partition) add a constant zero in each round, so they cancel in a within-run difference of sample accuracy or pass rates. But: (1) they dilute every change by the share of dead problems, 7–12% depending on the partition. Comparisons of decline size across seeds/partitions (e.g. 'the decline may grow with the rate on one seed', seed 1 vs seed 2) therefore carry partition-dependent dilution, and level comparisons across partitions carry offsets up to ~5 points (18 vs 11 dead problems). (2) Conditional and ratio measures do not cancel: matched finished accuracy, the finished/cap-share decomposition and the 'Fin. share' of Table 7, and r_t all include these problems. Their generations count as finished-but-wrong or cap-hit, so a change in termination on these problems moves 'finished accuracy' even though their correctness cannot change. (3) Under V′ they become scorable (46/51), so the 'cancellation' is exactly what makes original and re-scored changes differ (see the factor issue). The paper should state the number of dead problems per partition, and preferably report the main metrics with these problems excluded.

comments.title: Training limit of 512 tokens including the prompt, with a 512-new-token generation cap, means accepted examples are trained without their answer or EOS
comments.quote: with a training sequence limit of 512 tokens
comments.explanation:
Any kept solution can be up to 512 generated tokens, but the training sequence (prompt + solution) is cut at 512. With standard right-truncation, every kept solution longer than 512 − (prompt length) loses its ending: the final \boxed answer and the end-of-turn/EOS token. The summary reports 24–26% of the pool truncated. Two consequences matter for the paper's claims. (a) For a quarter of the pool, the verifier filter does not actually decide what is trained on: the trained text no longer contains the verified answer, so these are not 'kept correct solutions' in the GVT sense. (b) Training on sequences that stop mid-solution without EOS directly teaches non-termination. That is a plausible mechanism for the cap-hit increases at 5e-4 that §4.5 decomposes, and a design-induced cause of decline rather than a property of self-training. The paper does test this partly (one 1024-limit run and one retrain without truncated examples, both at seed 1, reported 'within the noise of single runs'). But the main configuration has the flaw, no rationale is given for setting the limit equal to the generation cap, and the truncation side is not stated. It also matters that the 1024-limit run (−5.7) is closer to the same-configuration replicate (−5.2) than to the original (−8.3). The method should state truncation side and EOS handling, give the truncation rate per run, and either fix the limit or treat it as a named confound in the conclusions about decline.

Related: Loss over the prompt is an unjustified, unablated design choice that interacts with duplicate problems and with the token budget — Computing loss on the prompt departs from standard rejection-sampling SFT (completion-only loss), and no reason is given. In this setup a problem can contribute up to k accepted solutions, so its statement and the fixed instruction are trained up to k times per round. At 5e-4 this adds a strong gradient signal unrelated to solving and invites memorising the problem text. It also uses part of the 512-token training budget, which worsens truncation of the solution. Because the paper attributes declines at high learning rates to self-training dynamics (less accurate finished solutions, more cap-hits), a training-objective choice that could itself cause degradation should be justified or ablated, or at least listed among the confounds. The paper should also state the per-round count of duplicate problems and whether samples were deduplicated.

comments.title: Reproducibility gaps: what a 'seed' controls, where replicate nondeterminism comes from, shared round-0 generations, and the inference setup
comments.quote: A “seed” sets the exam partition, the selection set and the training
comments.explanation: A seed is said to fix the partition, the selection set and the training randomness. Yet a 'same-configuration' replicate (Run A, 5e-4, seed 1) ends 3.2 points away, and Runs A and B at seed 2 have identical round-0 pools (424) but end 7.3 points apart in pass@1. If training and sampling were fully seeded, identical pools would give identical round-1 adapters. So something is not controlled (fp16 GPU nondeterminism, unseeded or batch-dependent sampling, data-loader order). The paper never says what, although these replicate gaps are used to calibrate training-seed variance. Also unstated: whether round-0 generations are produced once and shared across runs with the same seed (Tables 4 and 6 show identical R0 values 33.3/50.0/33.7 across three rates, which suggests they are); the generation engine and batching/padding (HF generate vs vLLM, fp16); whether the chat template's default system prompt is included; whether multiple accepted samples of the same problem are deduplicated; truncation side; and how cap-hit was recorded (re-tokenising to ≥508 rather than using the generation's finish reason is an approximation and should be justified). These details decide whether the runs can be reproduced, and they bear directly on the paper's noise arguments.

comments.title: All headline numbers are graded by a verifier known to reject ~1/6 of correct answers; 'the loop trained with it' does not justify using it as the evaluation measure
comments.quote: “Correct” always means accepted by the verifier (preset reward), the
comments.explanation: The same verifier V selects training data and grades the held-out exam. The paper then finds that V rejects 15.5–18.4% of V′-accepted generations, yet keeps V in every table, 'since that is the verifier the loop trained with'. That is a reason to use V for selection, not for measuring mathematical ability, which is the research question. For the 'no gain' claim, grading with V is partly conservative: adaptation to V would raise V-scores, so an absence of V-gains is informative. But for magnitudes (declines, finished-accuracy losses, the decomposition, the 2.2 bound), the better-calibrated grader should be primary, or both should be shown side by side. Re-scoring is cheap (saved generations, CPU-only), and only five runs were re-scored, so the conclusions that all other declines 'would also survive a re-score' rest on extrapolation from three. Re-scoring all runs with V′, plus an independent check (e.g. the scripted normaliser), would remove most of the factor/extrapolation issues above.

comments.title: The illustrative example of the gold-storage defect is written backwards
comments.quote: so a correct boxed prediction can fail against a bare gold (e.g. \frac43
comments.explanation: The sentence describes a boxed prediction failing against a bare gold, but the example reads '\frac43 against \boxed{\frac{4}{3}}', which shows a bare form against a boxed one, apparently the other way round. It is also not clear which of \frac43 / \frac{4}{3} is the stored gold. Appendix B's mechanism ('the bare gold is parsed to its first number') makes this matter: for gold '\frac43' the first number would be 4, so a correct 4/3 would fail and a wrong '4' would pass. That is the false-positive channel raised in a separate comment. A precise example (stored gold string, prediction string, what each side parses to) would remove the ambiguity.

comments.title: Abstract states post hoc results without the post hoc label the body attaches to them
comments.quote: gains above 2.2 points, a loose bound that omits training-seed variance.
comments.explanation: §3.4 says that claims resting on sample accuracy, 'including the 2.2-point bound, are therefore post hoc in the choice of measure'. §4.5 calls the finished-accuracy analysis 'post hoc and descriptive', and App H says the matched metric 'conditions on an outcome of training and is descriptive, not a causal effect'. The abstract qualifies the 2.2-point bound only for seed variance, not for the post hoc choice of measure or the lack of an equivalence margin. It also gives 'finished solutions become 5–11 points less accurate' as a plain headline finding, with no mention that it comes from a post hoc, post-treatment-conditioned metric. That metric drops 22–45 problems per run and uses a baseline that App H admits is biased for 6–21 problems. The abstract does label the r_t test 'post hoc', so the labelling is inconsistent. The paper applies its own standard of marking post hoc analyses in the body but relaxes it exactly where readers look first.

comments.title: 'Five of six runs' counts near-replicates and runs that share a baseline as independent evidence
comments.quote: vals excluding zero in five of six runs, while the cap-hit share rises 2–14 points.
comments.explanation: The six 5×10^-4 MATH-500 runs (A, B, no-filter at seeds 1 and 2) come from only two exam partitions. Within a seed, all three share the same round-0 generations, so the matched baseline is shared, and A and B share almost all of their pool. §4.4 says correctly that 'same-seed A and B are closer to two replicates than four', and App E/I.1 make the same point for A and B at seed 0 at 10^-5. §4.5 and I.1 still report 'five of six' as if it were six independent confirmations; the same goes for the cap-hit statement 'in all three seed-2 runs'. Since seed sets the partition, these really amount to two partition-level observations with correlated intervals. Reporting them as 'both partitions' (with the per-seed pattern) would be consistent with the paper's own replicate accounting.

comments.title: The cap-share split by seed is called 'qualitative' and possibly partition noise in App H, but is said to move the reading in §5.3
comments.quote: the split moves the reading: at 5 × 10−4 the cap share accounts for 12–30% of
comments.explanation: App H says the finished-accuracy shares 'have wide intervals' (e.g. 59% [−11, 114], 73% [43, 108]), that they split by seed, that 'this may be partition variation', and that 'What the table supports is qualitative'. §5.3(ii), the proposed audit protocol, and I.1 nonetheless present 12–30% versus 52–72% as a substantive finding that 'moves the reading'. These are ratios of two noisy differences, which are unstable when the total change is small (A, seed 2: −4.7), and the seed-1 and seed-2 intervals overlap. The ranges are point estimates over near-replicate runs (see the five-of-six comment). §5.3 should carry the App H caveat, or report the cap-share part in points with intervals rather than as a percentage of the decline.

comments.title: The 'about four of 76 by chance' heuristic is misapplied and used one-sidedly
comments.quote: at the 95% level about four of the 76 would exclude zero by chance if nothing
comments.explanation: The expected count of 76×0.05 ≈ 4 assumes the global null holds for all 76 intervals. Many are plainly non-null: train-on-gold (−18 to −26), Run C (−12 to −22), and most 5×10^-4 rows. The number of intervals for which 'nothing changed' is plausible is much smaller, so the expected count of false exclusions among them is lower, about 1–2 if roughly 30 are near-null. The count also includes the post hoc matched column, which uses a different re-scoring and 2,000 resamples. App E uses the heuristic to discount the 10^-5 seed-0 declines, but the multiplicity argument is not turned on the no-gain conclusion. There, the relevant issue is that the reported bound is the maximum of about 13 upper ends, so its joint coverage is below nominal. A family-wise or false-discovery-rate adjustment over a defined family (e.g. the 13 self-training Δsample-acc intervals), or a pooled analysis, would apply the multiplicity standard in both directions.

comments.title: 'Fixed in advance' covers the measures only: the design itself (rates, k, rounds, controls) was adaptive, and no registration record is given
comments.quote: Because 10−5 changed the MATH-500 outputs little, we reran Run A at 10−4
comments.explanation: The introduction says four measures and a reading rule were 'fixed in advance', which suggests pre-registration. No registration or timestamped protocol is cited. The learning-rate grid, the switch to k=4 and three rounds, the controls and the replicate were all chosen after seeing the 10^-5 results, and the primary measure, the cap-hit definition, the matched metric, the decomposition and the r_t test were all added afterwards. The paper is admirably open about most of these individually. Still, a headline such as 'no gain at four learning rates' comes from a sequence of data-dependent design choices, and Δpass@k mixes k=8 (10^-5) with k=4 (other rates). One sentence stating that only pass@1, pass@k, \boxed share and transitions plus the reading rule were pre-set, and that the rest of the design was adaptive, would prevent readers from crediting the study with more pre-specification than it had.
